query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Lightweight HEAs attain their unique combination of low density, high strength, and environmental resistance because a uniformly distributed solid‐solution matrix composed of lightweight elements (e.g., Al, Ti, V, Nb) produces significant lattice strain that both impedes dislocation motion and promotes the in situ formation of a dense, self-healing oxide film (rich in Al and/or Cr). In contrast, introducing elements that cause local segregation (e.g., small Cu additions) disrupts these effects and degrades performance.
generation.material_initial_state: A lightweight high‐entropy alloy with a near‐equimolar, homogeneous solid solution of low-density elements (e.g., an optimized AlTiVNb composition).
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled compositional change by adding a minor amount of an element (such as Cu) known to induce elemental segregation.
generation.conditions: Testing under high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., ~900°C) and corrosive environments (e.g., 0.6 M NaCl), as well as under mechanical loading typical of aerospace or rail-transport applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform solid-solution microstructure that confers coherent lattice strain combined with the formation of a continuous, passivating oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: The high atomic size mismatch among the low-density constituents generates lattice strain that both enhances strength by impeding dislocation motion and modifies diffusion pathways to favor the rapid formation of an adherent, self-healing oxide film. When compositional homogeneity is disrupted by segregation (e.g., by Cu addition), these synergistic benefits are diminished due to localized variations in lattice strain and discontinuous oxide coverage.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline homogeneous alloy, the modified alloy with induced segregation is predicted to show lower yield strength and ductility, a higher oxidation rate at high temperature, and a higher corrosion current density in saline environments.
generation.baseline: An optimized, homogeneous lightweight HEA (e.g., AlTiVNb) that exhibits uniform lattice strain and a continuous passivating oxide film.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis may cease to hold under conditions where the kinetics of oxide film formation are negligible (e.g., very low oxygen partial pressures) or where temperatures exceed the stability range for the solid-solution phase, leading to phase transformations that override the benefits of lattice strain and passivation.
generation.uncertainty: The relative quantitative contributions of lattice strain versus oxide film formation to the overall mechanical and environmental performance remain unclear and may vary with composition and processing routes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set using an optimized homogeneous composition (e.g., AlTiVNb) and another set with a controlled addition of Cu to induce elemental segregation. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., at 900°C), corrosion tests in 0.6 M NaCl solution, and mechanical strength measurements (e.g., tensile tests).
measurements: Phase homogeneity and segregation characterization via microscopy and spectroscopy
Oxidation kinetics (e.g., weight gain or oxide scale thickness analysis)
Corrosion performance using potentiodynamic polarization to measure corrosion current density
Mechanical properties including yield strength and ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-doped (segregated) alloy exhibits mechanical strength, oxidation resistance, and corrosion performance that are statistically indistinguishable from those of the homogeneous baseline alloy, this would falsify the hypothesis that uniform lattice strain and continuous oxide formation are critical for the targeted properties.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys, also known as HEAs, are generally composed of five or more elements in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios. These alloys are stable in a disordered solid solution state owing to a high mixing entropy [,]. Over the past twenty years, there has been an explosion of interest in a novel concept of alloy design that allows for the creation of materials with superior mechanical or physical properties. These properties include high yield strengths, ductility, and fracture toughness, in addition to superior high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance. As a result of these features, HEAs have found applications in a huge range of different fields [,,,,,,,,,,]. However, despite the application potential being high, the high density of many HEAs greatly inhibits the actual deployment of these applications. For example, the density of a CoCrFeNiMn HEA is 8.1 g/cm3, while the density of refractory high-enthalpy alloys (HEAs) is more than 10 g/cm3. Both of these HEAs have a mass density that is higher than that of steel, which has a density of 7.9 g per cubic centimeter. This study synthesized FeNiCuAlX high-entropy alloys (HEAs) (where X = Cr, Co, Mn) using arc melting and investigated their high-temperature oxidation behavior in air at 900 °C. The oxidation kinetics of all alloys followed a parabolic rate, with the oxidation rate constants (kp) of FeNiCuAlCr, FeNiCuAlCo, and FeNiCuAlMn being approximately two to three orders of magnitude lower than that of the FeNiCu alloy. Specifically, FeNiCuAlCr exhibited the lowest kp value of 1.72 × 10−6 mg2·cm4/s, which is significantly lower than those of FeNiCuAlCo (3.29 × 10−6 mg2·cm4/s) and FeNiCuAlMn (1.71 × 10−5 mg2·cm4/s). This suggests that the addition of chromium promotes the formation of a dense Al2O3/Cr2O3 oxide layer, significantly enhancing the oxidation resistance. Furthermore, corrosion resistance was assessed through potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy in a 3.5% NaCl solution. FeNiCuAlCr demonstrated exceptional resistance to localized corrosion, as indicated by its low corrosion current density (45.7 μA/cm2) and high pitting potential (−0.21 V), highlighting its superior corrosion performance.

However, the strong HEA films mentioned above suffer from low ductility in general. How to balance the strength and ductility of amorphous HEA films is important for their applications in the field of flexible microelectronic devices and mechanical metamaterials. In addition, seeking a high-performance HEA film with low density and corrosion resistance is of great significance for their applications in extreme conditions. In these cases, it is crucial to develop a high hardness, high strength–ductility synergy, and excellent corrosion resistance of amorphous lightweight high entropy alloy film. In this work, the lightweight AlTiVNb HEA film was prepared by magnetron sputtering, and the microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance were investigated.
